topics: 💍 The Rapist's Divorce — testing Abaye and Rava against 'all his days'
🫒 Teruma From Poor for Choice Produce — an effective transgression
🌾 Teruma Across Types — an ineffective one, and why
🐐 Temurah's Own Verse — 'both it and its substitute shall be holy'
👑 A Widow to the High Priest, a Blemished Animal to the Altar — two more test cases
⚖️ The Method: Every Mishna Becomes Evidence for One Side

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Testing 'Does a Forbidden Act Take Effect?'
overview.subtitle: Temurah 5a–5b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Having introduced the dispute between Abaye (a forbidden act still takes effect) and Rava (it accomplishes nothing; the lashes alone punish the transgression), the Gemara runs an extended series of test cases through both positions: the rapist forced to remarry his divorced victim, teruma separated from poor produce to cover choice produce, teruma separated across different crop types, consecrating a blemished animal, a widow's marriage to a High Priest, and — central to the tractate — temurah itself, whose verse 'both it and its substitute shall be holy' becomes Rava's own proof that substitution is a special case where the Torah explicitly makes the act effective. Each time a mishna seems to refute one opinion, the Gemara finds a specific verse that limits that ruling to its own case, restoring the general rule.

slides.title: 💍 First Test Case: The Rapist Who Divorced His Victim
slides.subtitle: Deuteronomy 22:29, 'he may not send her away all his days'

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: An Israelite rapist who divorces his victim remarries her and is not flogged. If Rava is right that transgressions are always effective, shouldn't the divorce have worked, making him liable for divorcing her?

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: It's different there — the verse says 'all his days,' teaching that he remains bound to remarry her forever. Since he must undo it, the divorce is treated as if it never fully took hold, so no lashes.

lines.speaker: For Abaye
lines.text: And what does 'all his days' teach you, who already says the act works? Without it, I would think he may choose whether or not to remarry her.

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: 'All his days' teaches that remarriage is obligatory, not merely available — a distinct halakha for each opinion.

callout.label: Pattern to watch:
callout.text: This exchange sets the template for the whole daf: a mishna seemingly refutes one opinion, and a specific verse rescues it as a special case.

slides.title: 🫒🌾 More Test Cases: Effective or Not?
slides.subtitle: Each mishna's outcome is matched to a verse that limits it to its own halakha
rows: Teruma from poor produce for choice produce
"You shall bear no sin by reason of it" (Num. 18:32) — 'sin' implies it must have consecrated status
Teruma from one crop type for another
"The first part of them" (Num. 18:12, repeated) — 'reishit' for each type separately
Redeeming an item devoted (ḥerem) to a priest
Not effective — given straight to the priest
"It is most holy" (Lev. 27:28) — 'as it is, it shall remain'
"From all your tithes you shall set apart" (Num. 18:29) — teaches effectiveness regardless of order

callout.label: Note the symmetry:
callout.text: Whichever way the mishna rules, that side's proponent must show the ruling is a special exception, not a refutation of the general theory.

slides.title: 🐐 Temurah Becomes the Test Case
slides.subtitle: The tractate's own verse settles a piece of the Abaye–Rava debate

nodes.content: ❓ Substitution is forbidden, yet the mishna says it takes effect and the animal becomes holy — doesn't this refute Rava?
📜 Rava answers: the very same verse states explicitly, וְהָיָה הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ יִהְיֶה קֹּדֶשׁ — 'both it and its substitute shall be holy'
✅ This is a Torah-stated exception: temurah's effectiveness is not proof that forbidden acts work generally, only that this specific forbidden act does
🤔 And for Abaye, who needs no special verse for effectiveness? He reads 'הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ' as teaching something else: that the original animal retains its sanctity too (not just the substitute)

callout.label: Why it matters:
callout.text: Temurah is the paradigm case for the whole sugya — the one place the Torah spells out in so many words that a forbidden substitution 'sticks.'

slides.title: 👑 Two More Cases, Two More Special Verses
slides.subtitle: A widow's marriage to a High Priest; a blemished animal consecrated for the altar

boxes.title: Widow to High Priest
items: Forbidden (Lev. 21:14–15), yet the marriage IS valid — offspring follows the 'flawed' status
Rava: "he shall not profane his seed" (לֹא יְחַלֵּל) implies the union took effect enough to produce a profaned child
For Abaye: the doubled language teaches two profanations — for him and for her

boxes.title: Blemished Animal to Altar
items: Rava: "for a vow it shall not be accepted" (לֹא יֵרָצֶה) — only its sacrifice fails, so consecration itself succeeded
For Abaye: without this verse, one might think the blemished offering could even be sacrificed

callout.label: Method repeats:
callout.text: In case after case, Rava needs to locate the verse that makes an exception; Abaye needs to locate the verse teaching some other detail.

slides.title: ⚖️ The Sugya's Method, Step by Step
slides.subtitle: How the Gemara tests a general theory against many mishnayot

steps.content: 1️⃣ A mishna rules that a forbidden act either succeeded or failed
2️⃣ If it succeeded, this seems to refute Rava (nothing forbidden should work)
3️⃣ If it failed, this seems to refute Abaye (everything forbidden should work)
4️⃣ Each time, the challenged sage points to a verse unique to that halakha, preserving his general rule as the default everywhere else

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: By the end of this sugya, temurah stands as Rava's own proof-text — the one forbidden act the Torah says outright takes effect.

summary.principle: Across many test cases — the rapist's remarriage, teruma, ḥerem, a High Priest's marriage, a blemished offering, and temurah itself — the Gemara shows that whichever side (Abaye: effective; Rava: ineffective) a mishna seems to refute, a specific verse limits that ruling to its own case.

flowSteps.content: 💍 Rapist's divorce not effective — 'all his days' forces remarriage
🫒🌾 Teruma cases split: bad-for-good works, cross-type doesn't — each has its own verse

columns.content: 🐐 Temurah: 'הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ' proves this forbidden act specifically works
👑 Widow/blemished-animal cases each get their own reconciling verse

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: no single rule governs all forbidden acts — each halakha's own verse decides whether it 'took'

quiz.q: According to Rava, why is the Israelite rapist not flogged for divorcing his victim, even though he transgressed a prohibition?
o: Because rape carries no prohibition
Because 'all his days' (Deut. 22:29) shows the divorce never fully took hold, since he remains bound to remarry her
Because he is exempt as a minor
Because only priests are flogged for this
quiz.e: Rava explains that 'all his days' teaches the obligation to remarry persists indefinitely, meaning the divorce is treated as not having fully severed the marriage — hence no lashes.

quiz.q: What verse does the Gemara use to show that separating teruma from poor-quality produce to cover choice produce is nonetheless effective?
o: "You shall bear no sin by reason of it" (Num. 18:32)
"It is most holy" (Lev. 27:28)
"He shall not profane his seed" (Lev. 21:15)
"For a vow it shall not be accepted" (Lev. 22:23)
quiz.e: Rabbi Ile'a derives from 'you shall bear no sin by reason of it' that the act must have consecrated the produce as teruma — otherwise there would be no sin to bear.

quiz.q: Which verse does Rava cite as proof that temurah is a Torah-stated exception where a forbidden act does take effect?
o: "Reishit" — the first part of them
"He shall not exchange it, nor substitute it"
"Both it and that for which it is substituted shall be holy" (הוּא וּתְמוּרָתוֹ)
"It shall not be redeemed"
quiz.e: Rava points to the mishna's own verse, 'both it and its substitute shall be holy,' as explicit textual proof that this particular forbidden act (substitution) is effective — not evidence for a general rule.

quiz.q: In the case of consecrating a blemished animal for the altar, how does Rava explain why the mishna calls the consecration effective, seemingly against his general rule?
o: He says the mishna is simply wrong
"For a vow it shall not be accepted" (לֹא יֵרָצֶה) implies only the sacrifice fails, so the consecration itself succeeded
Blemished animals were never really forbidden
He agrees with Abaye entirely here
quiz.e: Rava reads the specific wording — that only its acceptance/sacrifice (ritzui) is barred — as proof that consecration itself took effect, making this a limited exception rather than a refutation of his rule.

quiz.q: What is the general pattern the Gemara follows throughout this sugya when a mishna seems to contradict either Abaye or Rava?
o: The Gemara simply declares the mishna corrupt
It finds a verse specific to that halakha that limits the ruling to its own case, preserving the sage's general theory elsewhere
It always sides with Abaye
It ignores mishnayot entirely
quiz.e: Time and again, whichever sage's rule a mishna appears to contradict, the Gemara locates language in that specific verse that explains the ruling as a unique exception, leaving the broader theory intact.
